newsitem.title: USA: Middlesex County, Mass., in rare municipal default.
newsitem.headline: Middlesex County, Mass., in rare municipal default.

text.p: Middlesex County, Mass., home of Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, defaulted Friday on $4.5 million of debt, the county's creditors and state officials said.

The default, which one state official said was "the first time in memory" a local government in Massachusetts missed debt payments, came after the state rejected a last-minute attempt by the county to borrow even more money to pay off its creditors.
Fleet Financial Group and The Boston Co. confirmed that their notes had not been paid by Friday's due date.

A spokesman for Fleet, James Mahoney, said the bank expected to be officially notified on Monday of default on the $1.5 million in county notes it holds. "We're reserving the right to initiate legal remedies," Mahoney said.
Vincent Loporchio, a spokesman for The Boston Co., said the bank was owed $3 million that went unpaid Friday. "We're hopeful that the situation will be resolved soon," Loporchio said.
County officials did not return telephone calls Friday.
Defaults in the nation's $1.3 trillion municipal bond market are extremely rare, variously estimated at about one or two percent of the overall market.

Even beleagured Orange County, Calif., which filed for bankrupty protection in December 1994, reached agreement with its noteholders to roll over its debt. Orange County, which emerged from bankruptcy earlier this year, said that meant it had not actually defaulted, though rating agency analysts disagreed on the distinction.

Paul Devine, assistant director at Moody's Investors Service, said Middlesex's situation "remains dire" even if an agreement was eventually reached with creditors to find an alternative payment schedule. That is because the county apparently does not have enough cash to pay all its creditors.
The county, which has a nearly $23 million budget, ran into into trouble with its county hospital which recently has been operating at just 25 percent capacity.

It has agreed to sell the facility to for-profit Olympus Healthcare Group Inc. of Westborough, Mass. for $4.4 million, but that will not be enough to cover the county's $17 million in hospital-associated liabilities.
Charles Baker, Massachusetts Secretary of Administration and Finance, blasted county officials for failing to address the situation in time to avert default.
"Default on public debt is inexcusable," Baker said. "We must promptly work together to insure this situation is not repeated."

Gov. William Weld has long called for the elimination of county-level government in Massachusetts, and some state officials privately speculated that the governor would use the Middlesex County crisis as a catalyst for such a move. The state typically bails out three to four of its counties each year at an annual cost of up to $6 million a year.
Eric Ferhnstrom, a spokesman for state Treasurer Joseph Malone, predicted there would be little immediate impact on the county's employees and residents.
"I would imagine life would go on in much the same way as Orange County after they went bankrupt."
